analysis.one_liner: Repeals the federal law requiring prevailing wages on federally funded construction.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee: introduced in June 2009 with 32 Republican cosponsors, it was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee and never received a vote before the 111th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Davis-Bacon Act requires contractors on federally financed construction of public buildings and public works to pay workers the locally prevailing wage for their trade. This bill would wipe out that requirement, effective 30 days after enactment, while leaving contracts already in place untouched. Its practical effect would be to let contractors on federal jobs pay whatever wage they choose, which would likely pull down pay for construction workers on those projects.
analysis.who_benefits: Construction contractors bidding on federally financed projects, especially those who pay less than the prevailing local wage, would gain by cutting labor costs. Government cost estimates and contractor associations have long argued prevailing-wage rules add to federal construction costs. Workers at the bottom of the wage scale might see slightly more job opportunities if labor gets cheaper, but the main gain is to employers' margins.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the Davis-Bacon Act, which requires the locally prevailing wage for laborers and mechanics on federally financed or assisted construction of public buildings and public works.
Repeals the related federal reporting requirements for contractors covered by the wage rules.
Takes effect 30 days after enactment but leaves existing contracts, and bids already outstanding, unaffected.

analysis.who_pays: Construction workers on federally funded projects would bear the cost, since the wage floor that keeps pay at the local prevailing rate would disappear. Local governments and unionized contractors that anchor wage standards in a region would also lose leverage. Taxpayers might save on some federal construction if bids fall, but the clearest cost is a pay cut risk for the workers themselves.

drawbacks.text: Repeal would remove the only federal requirement that workers on federally financed construction be paid the local prevailing wage, opening the door to lower pay on those jobs.
Supporters of repeal argue prevailing-wage rules inflate federal construction costs and impose paperwork burdens on contractors; that tradeoff is the honest core of the dispute.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The savings to taxpayers are real but modest and uncertain, while the wage floor protects several million dollars of pay per project for skilled trades workers and helps keep low-road contractors from undercutting local wage standards. The bill offered no replacement protection for workers, so its costs fall directly on the people Davis-Bacon was written to protect.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up, so it died when the Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve King of Iowa, joined by Rep. Connie Mack, introduced the Davis-Bacon Repeal Act on June 16, 2009.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor on the day of introduction.
Thirty-two House Republicans cosponsored the bill; no Democrat did.
No further action was taken: the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and expired when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Construction workers on federally funded projects are better off because the bill died, since the prevailing-wage floor stayed in place. Contractors hoping to cut labor costs on federal jobs gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal construction workers kept their wage floor

for.name: Rep. Steve King
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the Davis-Bacon Act and referred it to committee.

against.name: Rep. George Miller
against.role: Chair, House Education and Labor Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for committee action; it received no hearing or vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All 32 cosponsors were Republicans, and the Democratic-controlled committee that would have considered it took no action.

industries.note: Repeal would let them pay below the prevailing local wage on federally financed work, cutting their labor costs directly out of workers' pay. Cheaper bids might pass some savings to taxpayers, but the primary gain is contractor margin.

The prevailing-wage floor is what keeps nonunion low-wage bidders from undercutting area standards on federal jobs. Repeal would erode that floor and weaken the leverage that maintains regional wage norms.
